newsitem.title: UK: Foreign policy becoming more parochial, says IISS.
newsitem.headline: Foreign policy becoming more parochial, says IISS.

text.p: The world's major powers are rapidly losing interest in foreign and security affairs as they become obsessed with domestic politics, a leading European think-tank said on Thursday.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in its Strategic Survey for 1996/7 that the new trend meant prospects for multilateral diplomacy had worsened sharply since the end of the Cold War.
"Throughout the world in 1996, foreign and security affairs were driven by a pervasive and persistent parochialism," said the introduction to the IISS report.

"Governments found themselves preoccupied with domestic considerations...in their search for votes, or for support, leaders vying for the top position adjusted their policies to reflect what they thought their constituents wanted."

This focus on internal affairs meant it was unlikely the United States and European powers would commit themselves to politically risky initiatives such as sending troops to help restore order in distant troublespots or to prevent famines.
"The Cold War tendency to see core interests indirectly at stake in distant parts of the globe has now totally eroded," the report said.

"Comfortably cocooned in their own sense of security, citizens of democratic countries are in no mood to sacrifice their well-being for supposed international advantage, nor to rally to the service of a purely humanitarian goal."

When foreign policy did make the agenda it tended to be subservient to domestic needs, as U.S. President Bill Clinton showed in the 1996 election race when he was trying to placate both his adversaries in Congress and the electorate.

A prime example was U.S. moves to punish foreign companies doing business with Cuba, Libya and Iran, which the report said underscored just how far the international community had to go before effective multilateralism could be considered anything other than a pretence.

The most contentious piece of U.S. legislation was the the Helms-Burton act -- allowing foreign companies doing business with Cuba to be punished -- which sparked fierce protests from Canada and the European Union.
"Foreign policy, like domestic policy, now has a twin meaning, and this is perhaps one of the genuinely new characteristics of the post-Cold War world," said the report.
"In some way or another, domestic politics has become the concern of other countries, even if that concern does not always translate into action."

Washington's refusal to support United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in his bid to secure a second term in office "dented hopes for a world in which multilateral concepts have priority over parochial domestic factionalism."

The report accused the European Union of adopting the same attitude as it struggled to boost integration between its 15 nations. "While the 'under construction' signs were up, the Europeans barely lifted their gaze above their own ramparts," it said.
